claims.text: A carefully balanced multi-principal-element composition produces a chemically disordered solid solution in lightweight high-entropy alloys.
The chemically disordered solid solution enables solid-solution strengthening.
The balanced composition promotes uniform formation of a stable, protective oxide layer.
Disrupting the compositional balance degrades mechanical strength.
Disrupting the compositional balance degrades corrosion resistance.
Disrupting the compositional balance degrades high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Changing the concentration of one principal element perturbs chemical homogeneity.
Chemical disorder facilitates formation of a uniform, adherent oxide layer.
Composition-induced lattice distortions impede dislocation motion.
The multi-principal-element composition enables early and uniform formation of a protective oxide film.
Relative to the baseline alloy, a compositionally disturbed alloy will have lower yield strength.
Relative to the baseline alloy, a compositionally disturbed alloy will have a higher corrosion rate.
Relative to the baseline alloy, a compositionally disturbed alloy will form a less effective high-temperature oxide layer.
The proposed mechanism should apply under service temperatures up to about 800°C and in standard corrosive environments.
At temperatures above approximately 900–1000°C or in overly aggressive media, the protective oxide layer may fail regardless of compositional balance.
The comparison uses an optimized balanced alloy as a control and an alloy with a controlled reduction in one key principal element.
Failure of the modified alloy to show the predicted statistically significant performance degradation would falsify the proposed mechanism.
